Burnout is classified by the World Health Organization as an occupational phenomenon rather than a medical condition, a distinction that constrains what an automated system may legitimately claim. Detection in practice rests on periodic self-report inventories, administered infrequently, vulnerable to response bias, and silent on why a score was produced. Neural classifiers widen coverage but substitute one form of opacity for another. This paper presents a burnout detection system that separates measurement from explanation and enforces that separation architecturally. A four-stage pipeline scores workplace communication using a transformer sentiment classifier, a word-emotion lexicon and surface behavioural features, combined by a transparent additive rule in which every point is attributable to a named signal by construction. A retrieval-augmented language model then explains those scores and returns the specific records supporting each statement, so that a reader can check the reasoning rather than trust it. The two stages communicate through a single read-only file, which keeps the scoring stage authoritative and leaves the language model no means of altering a risk band. The implementation is verified by 151 automated tests and degrades to a rule-based analysis with explicit disclosure when generation is unavailable; of ten integration defects identified, six were repaired and four are documented as open. A quantum machine learning study conducted in two independent frameworks is reported alongside: the quantum kernel reproduces the classical result exactly at four orders of magnitude greater cost, and an analytical derivation shows why the chosen encoding determined that outcome in advance.

One classification is clearly incorrect. The message "Today was an average day" is labelled Negative at a confidence of 0.662, and contributes two points to a burnout score on that basis. The utterance is neutral by any reasonable reading. The error is attributable to domain mismatch: the classifier is pre-trained and fine-tuned on Twitter data [7], a register in which affective expression is markedly stronger than in neutral workplace correspondence, so that the decision boundary between neutral and negative is displaced when transferred to this domain. The low confidence associated with this and the other negative classifications is a visible symptom of that displacement, and is the strongest available argument for incorporating the retained confidence value into the scoring formula rather than discarding it after the label is assigned.

All results are obtained on the committed ten-record corpus. Encoding runs on CPU by default, with optional Metal or CUDA acceleration that falls back to CPU with a logged warning when unavailable, so one collaborator's device setting cannot break the service for another. Generation defaults to a local model at temperature 0.2, 1600 output tokens and a 120-second timeout; retrieval depth defaults to five, capped at twenty-five; the 180-second interface timeout must exceed the generation timeout, or the dashboard aborts mid-generation. The quantum study is configured separately: six attributes on six qubits, two variational layers with ring entanglement, 24 trainable parameters, no dimensionality reduction. Quantum results are obtained on state-vector simulators under PennyLane 0.45.1 and Qiskit 2.5.2 with qiskit-machine-learning 0.9.1 on Python 3.14, over 1,500 sampled rows split 1,125 train and 375 test, with the quantum kernel capped at 400 training rows, and are additionally executed with finite-shot sampling on the Qniverse platform [20].

Evaluation on the committed ten-record corpus is reported in full and is candidly insufficient to support generalisation. It does establish that the attribution property holds, that the degradation path functions, and that the architecture surfaces defects rather than absorbing them: six integration defects were identified and repaired, and four upstream defects documented and tolerated without fabricating the measurements they suppressed. In a system whose output concerns identified individuals, preserving the distinction between absent and zero, and never letting a fluent generator overrule an accountable measurement, is the substantive contribution. The accompanying quantum study reaches a null result and explains it: the encoding adopted yields a kernel that factorises into a classically computable product, so its agreement with the classical kernel was determined by construction rather than discovered by experiment. Reporting that derivation, rather than the accuracy figure alone, is what makes the comparison informative.

Encoding uses all-MiniLM-L6-v2, a six-layer sentence transformer producing 384-dimensional vectors from an eighty-megabyte model [14]. Three implementation properties are consequential. Vectors are L2-normalised at encode time, reducing cosine similarity to a dot product and, with a cosine-configured index, making the returned distance exactly one minus similarity: a bounded relevance score in the unit interval, rather than an unbounded distance that means nothing on a dashboard. The model loads lazily behind a double-checked lock, since loading at import time would fetch eighty megabytes during test collection and load two copies under concurrent first requests. The class implements the embedding interface without importing the orchestration framework, so a framework version change cannot break encoding.

Retrieval takes the question, optionally applies a metadata filter, and returns the k closest records with their similarity. Three details matter. An employee identifier named in the question is recognised by a regular expression tolerant of separator and spacing variants and normalised to the zero-padded canonical form, so that it matches the synthesised identifiers. Multiple filter conditions are combined under an explicit conjunction, because the store otherwise treats them as a multi-key lookup and applies only one; a single condition is emitted without the conjunction, which some versions reject. Depth is clamped to between one and twenty-five, so that an excessive request cannot overflow the provider's context window.

The system prompt serves four roles, each answering a distinct failure mode. It requires every sentence to rest on the supplied records and forbids inventing employees, quotes, dates, events, job titles or metrics, since an invented detail could send a manager to discuss something that never happened. It forbids re-deriving the risk level, requiring the label to be echoed verbatim, since a silently disagreeing classifier would put the dashboard and the model at odds. It forbids diagnostic and clinical vocabulary, consistent with the occupational rather than medical framing [1]. And it declares record text to be data rather than instruction, so that a message containing commands is read as evidence about its author.

The system prompt serves four roles, each answering a failure mode. Every sentence must rest on the supplied records: no invented employees, quotes, dates, events, job titles or metrics, since an invented detail could send a manager to discuss something that never happened. The risk level may not be re-derived and must be echoed verbatim, since a silently disagreeing classifier would put dashboard and model at odds. Diagnostic and clinical vocabulary is forbidden, consistent with the occupational rather than medical framing [1]. And record text is declared data rather than instruction, so a message containing commands is read as evidence about its author.

Four classical baselines — majority-class, logistic regression, a support vector machine with radial basis function kernel, and a random forest — are evaluated against two quantum models: a variational quantum classifier and a quantum kernel support vector machine. The quantum kernel is the state fidelity between encoded samples, supplied as a precomputed Gram matrix to the same support vector classifier used for the classical radial basis function model [17]. Optimiser, regularisation constant, random seed and split are identical across both, so the kernel matrix is the only quantity that differs. That is why the support vector machine, not the variational classifier, is the appropriate vehicle: its objective is convex, so the solution is a deterministic function of the Gram matrix alone, with no initialisation or local minima to confound the result.

The result is reported because it locates the limitation correctly. A quantum advantage requires a feature map inducing a similarity structure that is both informative for the data and hard to compute classically. The second-order map of Havlíček et al. [16], which entangles rotations on products of attributes, satisfies the second condition; it is implemented here but not yet evaluated at scale. A further consideration is that the capacity of a kernel machine is governed by the margin relative to the data radius rather than by the dimension of the feature space, so the exponential dimension of the quantum Hilbert space confers no advantage in itself.

The committed corpus is datasets/sample.csv, a ten-row development set containing a single clean_text column of short workplace utterances. The sentiment script is written against datasets/processed/enron_clean.csv and truncates to the first thousand messages by an explicit development-mode statement; that file is absent from the repository, so the committed outputs derive from the ten-row sample. This is stated plainly because the distinction between the intended and the evaluated corpus materially bounds every result in Section VII.

Employee identity is entirely absent from the upstream data: the scored file is one row per message with no identifier. Since the dashboard must rank employees by risk and search per employee, identifiers are generated deterministically from the row number as EMP_0001, EMP_0002 and so on, zero-padded so that string sort order in dashboard tables matches numerical order. Determinism is the essential property; an identifier derived from ordering alone would not survive a restart. Should an actual employee_id column later appear, it is used in preference.
